card.title: Playing games
card.q: How does a button under your thumb move a world?

part.name: the controller
part.line: two sticks and eight buttons — every one a switch
part.blurb: Under every button is a switch, and a switch has two words: pressed and not pressed. The console never sees your thumbs; it reads a short row of ones and zeros, hundreds of times a second. Everything you ever do in the game arrives as that row, and as nothing else.

door.q: What happens between a thumb and a number?
A switch says one word — yes or no. Where does that lead?

part.name: the box under the television
part.line: a computer, wearing a costume
part.blurb: Take the case off and the parts are the same as in the phone and the laptop: a processor to follow instructions, memory to hold the world, a program saying what to do. The makers do not hide this — the processor’s name is printed on the box. A console is a computer whose program tells it to behave like a toy.

door.q: What is inside, and how does it follow a program?
Who keeps the box in order while it plays?

part.name: the processor
part.line: billions of instructions a second, none of them clever
part.blurb: Sixty times every second the processor runs the same round: read the controller, move the world forward one step, work out what the world now looks like, hand the picture to the screen. Each of the billions of instructions is no cleverer than “add these two numbers”. The speed is astonishing; every single instruction is dumb.

door.q: How does it decide, sixty times a second, what happens next?
What are the billions of instructions made of?

part.name: memory
part.line: the world you move through, held in numbered cells
part.blurb: The city, your position in it, the score: all of it lives in memory, which is an enormous row of numbered cells, each holding a number. Change a cell and the world changes; the machine has no other way to be different. Cut the power and every cell forgets — which is why there is a save file, further down this trail.

door.q: How does a circuit hold the world you move through?
Where does the picture you see live?

part.name: the picture
part.line: two million lamps, each told how bright to be
part.blurb: The screen is a wall of tiny lamps, and each lamp is told, dozens of times a second, three numbers: how much red, how much green, how much blue. A frame of a game is about two million such trios, and the television is simply the machine obedient enough to display them. Nobody draws anything; numbers are obeyed.

door.q: How is a picture made, from lamp to number?
What holds two million lamps between the frames?

part.name: the shared world
part.line: two consoles, two copies, one truth to agree on
part.blurb: Play with someone far away and there is no single machine holding the world: there are two, each with its own copy, trading messages as fast as the wires allow. When two players grab the same object in the same instant, the copies disagree — and every trick the game’s programmers use to settle it descends from one old, hard question.

door.q: How do two machines share one world?
Two players, one world — what keeps it whole?

part.name: the save file
part.line: memory that survives the off switch
part.blurb: A save is a copy of the interesting cells, written onto a disk that does not forget when the power leaves. Switch on tomorrow and those numbers are read back into memory, and the world resumes exactly where it stopped. Nothing in the machine understands “saved game”; it is numbers copied faithfully from one kind of memory to another.

door.q: Who keeps the files, and who runs the machine?
How does anything survive the off switch?

card.bottom: Follow any part of this trail far enough down and it dissolves into switches: pressed and not pressed, high and low, 0 and 1. The trails below lead the rest of the way down; at their ends, the primers are waiting.

door.q: The choices that lead down to the gates
The trail that ends at the Bit

card.title: Delivering food
card.q: What happens between the tap and the doorbell?

part.name: the phone
part.line: a computer that happens to fit in a pocket
part.blurb: The phone is the same machine as the console and the laptop: a processor, memory, and programs that give it its habits. The glass is a fine invisible grid of wires; where your finger lands, one row and one column cross, and the machine is told a coordinate — two numbers — and nothing more. It has never seen a finger in its life.

door.q: What does the glass understand?
What is the phone saying, and to whom?

part.name: the app
part.line: a list of instructions, written down in advance
part.blurb: The app is not a place and not a person: it is a long list of instructions, written in advance and followed without opinion. Each tap hands it one new fact, and it answers with the next instruction on the list. Doorbells, spaceships and food apps are all the same arrangement — instructions, obeyed exactly.

door.q: What does “following an instruction” mean, exactly?
Who lets a hundred apps share one phone?

part.name: the restaurant’s side of the internet
part.line: a warehouse computer answering ten thousand strangers
part.blurb: Your tap becomes a small message, copied from your phone to a tower to a wire to a building full of computers — a server, which is a computer with no screen of its own, kept cool in a warehouse and answering ten thousand strangers at once. Your order lands in its memory like a note on a spike, and the reply — received — is copied back down the same road.

door.q: How does an order cross the wire to the warehouse?
Ten thousand strangers — how does it keep track?

part.name: the match
part.line: facts and rules, searched for the answer
part.blurb: Which restaurant, which rider: the assignment is made by a machine walking through facts — this rider is two kilometres away, that one is busy, this kitchen needs twenty minutes — hunting for the combination that satisfies all the rules at once. No person weighs the offers; the search does. Some of the most useful software ever written is exactly this, and it is a way of speaking to a machine, not a kind of hardware.

door.q: Can you tell a machine only facts, and still get answers?
Who decides which order goes first?

part.name: the route
part.line: a city as a picture the machine can walk
part.blurb: To the machine the city is not streets and houses but corners joined by edges, each edge with a length. The best route is found by a recipe that contains a copy of itself: the cheapest way to a far corner is built out of cheapest ways to nearer ones, the same step applied again and again until nothing remains. The machine has no idea what a street is. It never needs one.

door.q: What happens when a task contains a copy of itself?
How does the map reach the courier’s phone?

part.name: the courier’s phone
part.line: instructions, one word at a time
part.blurb: The courier’s phone speaks the way machines speak: one instruction at a time — left in two hundred metres, then arrive. The rider never sees the whole plan; they see the next word, and the next word is always enough. There is a whole tradition of computing built on exactly that discipline: a vocabulary of small words, each obeyed exactly, out of which anything can be composed.

door.q: Can a language be small enough to trust?
What is the phone saying to the dispatch?

part.name: one order, two riders
part.line: the bug the whole system exists to prevent
part.blurb: The dangerous moment is invisible: two couriers press accept on the same order in the same instant. Two hands, one memory cell, no agreed order — and a carelessly built system can hand one meal to two riders, or to none. Every ordering system on earth is, at bottom, a scheme for making that impossible.

door.q: What happens when two act on the same thing at once?
How does the order reach exactly one rider?

card.bottom: The phone, the app, the warehouse, the match: each is the same machine — switches, numbers, instructions — wearing different clothes. The trails below take those words one layer at a time; at their ends stand the primers, each one alone.

door.q: The trail that ends at a real machine
The trail that ends at the Bit

card.title: Watching movies
card.q: Where does a film live while you watch it?

part.name: the screen
part.line: two million lamps, each told what to be
part.blurb: A television picture is about two million tiny lamps, each given, dozens of times a second, three numbers: how much red, how much green, how much blue. A film is therefore a river of numbers arriving just in time to be shown, and the screen is the machine obedient enough to turn them into light. The pause button does not stop the world; it stops the numbers.

door.q: How is a picture made, from lamp to number?
What holds the picture between the beats?

part.name: the sound
part.line: your evening, measured 44,100 times a second
part.blurb: Sound reaches the ear as pressure in the air. A microphone measures it 44,100 times a second and writes each measurement down as a number; a speaker reads the numbers back and recreates the pressure. Music on a computer is a long column of numbers and nothing else — the screen’s trick, one dimension over.

door.q: How does a song become numbers, and back again?
Is a picture caught the same way?

part.name: the stream
part.line: a film poured through a wire, just in time
part.blurb: The numbers cannot all be sent at once, so they are poured: a few million bits a second, arriving shortly before they are needed. When more arrives than the wire can carry, the picture thins — grey blocks, a stutter — and that is the wire telling the truth about itself.

door.q: How does a film cross the wire, just in time?
Who keeps the film arriving just in time?

part.name: the buffer
part.line: the next minute of the film, parked in your living room
part.blurb: Because wires stutter, the player keeps a cushion: half a minute or so of the future, already arrived and held in memory. When the wire coughs, the film keeps playing out of the cushion, and the race between arrival and playback starts again quietly. The buffer is memory doing what memory exists to do: holding a state against time.

door.q: How does a circuit hold anything against time?
Why hold a copy until the far end answers?

part.name: the squeeze
part.line: a program that decides what your eye will not miss
part.blurb: Two million lamps repainted dozens of times a second is far more than any household wire can carry, so a program — the codec — compresses the numbers: this frame is nearly the last frame; this block of sky barely changes; the eye forgives. The film you see is the codec’s opinion of the film, computed on the fly, and it is a program like any other: instructions, obeyed exactly.

door.q: What exactly is being squeezed, and what is it made of?
The codec decides — what is deciding made of?

part.name: the buttons
part.line: a language of a dozen words
part.blurb: Play. Pause. Back ten seconds. The remote’s whole vocabulary is a dozen words, and the player obeys one at a time, in the order pressed, without ever guessing. It is the oldest arrangement in computing — a small vocabulary, exact obedience — and there are whole languages built on nothing but it.

door.q: Two whole languages made of almost nothing
Every button a switch — what do switches say?

part.name: the suggestions
part.line: facts about millions of evenings, walked to a guess
part.blurb: “Because you watched” is a machine searching recorded facts — millions of evenings, what was finished, what was abandoned — for what fits yours. It is not a person and it is not magic; it is search through relations, the same craft that assigns a rider to an order, run at planetary scale.

door.q: Facts about millions of evenings, walked to a guess
Where do the facts about evenings come from?

card.bottom: Lamps, pressure, wires, cushions: numbers all the way down, and numbers the machine can only hold and obey. The bottom of the deck explains how anything this obedient can also be this capable.

door.q: The trail that ends at the Bit and at memory
The trail that ends at the Bit

trail.title: How sound happens
trail.intro: Sound is pushes in the air. To keep a song, a machine must turn the pushes into numbers it can hold, and to play it, back again. This is the trail of that trick, from ear to number.

step.name: pressure
step.line: a wave of pushes in the air
step.blurb: Sound is pressure. A drum, a voice, a speaker cone pushes the air, the push travels as a wave, and your eardrum is shoved in time with it. A single note is the air swinging back and forth a few hundred times a second; nothing solid ever moves from the singer to you, only the push.

door.q: Is a picture caught the same way?
What does the wave become, in the end?

step.name: the diaphragm
step.line: a little drum that turns push into voltage
step.blurb: A microphone holds a tiny drum, thinner than a hair. Each arriving push bends it, the bending drags a magnet through a coil of wire, and the wire answers with a wobbling voltage: the push, copied as electricity. The wave is still continuous, still in time with the song.

door.q: Another sheet that turns a push into numbers?
Measured, rounded, numbered — the picture too?

step.name: sampling
step.line: measured 44,100 times every second
step.blurb: A machine cannot hold a continuous wobble, so it measures it: 44,100 quick snapshots every second, each one the voltage at that instant. The number is not arbitrary. The ear tops out near twenty thousand waves a second, and measuring at least twice per wave rebuilds every wave the ear can hear; the compact disc chose 44,100, and the number stayed.

door.q: Who gives the beat?
How is a measurement spelled?

step.name: rounding
step.line: each measurement, one of 65,536 steps
step.blurb: Each snapshot is rounded to the nearest of 65,536 steps and written down as a number. The rounding is honest — the true voltage is almost never exactly on a step — but the steps are so fine that the rebuilt wave is indistinguishable, to an ear, from the original. One rounded number is called a sample.

door.q: Pictures are caught the same way: measured, rounded, numbered.
65,536 steps — how is a step spelled?

step.name: the file
step.line: a small note, then millions of numbers
step.blurb: A WAV file is a small header — 44,100 a second, 16 bits per sample, two ears — followed by millions of samples in order, one per ear per moment. The file is a long column of numbers and a note about how to read it, and nothing else.

door.q: Where do millions of numbers wait?
Who keeps the files?

step.name: the bytes
step.line: each number spelled in sixteen binary digits
step.blurb: A sample can hold any of 65,536 values, and 65,536 is 2¹⁶, so each sample is spelled in sixteen binary digits, split into two bytes of eight. A three-minute song is some thirty million bytes: an entire performance pressed into a column of numbers, in the alphabet the whole machine speaks.

door.q: Where do the two symbols come from?
Where do the numbers park?

trail.bottom: Push to voltage, voltage to number, number to digits: this is how the machine keeps anything at all.

door.q: The Bit — the alphabet of two symbols
Memory — where a song waits while it plays

trail.title: How an image happens
trail.intro: A picture is a wall of lamps obeying numbers. To draw, the machine must turn light into numbers, numbers into memory, and memory back into light, in time. This is the trail, from lamp to number and back.

step.name: one lamp
step.line: told how much red, green and blue to be
step.blurb: One pixel is three lamps pressed close together: red, green, blue. Each is told, by a number, how brightly to shine, and the three mix in the eye — full of all three is white, none of them is black. That is the whole of colour on every screen you own.

door.q: Is sound caught the same way?
How bright is a number?

step.name: three numbers
step.line: a pixel is a trio, each 0 to 255
step.blurb: Each lamp’s brightness is rounded to one of 256 steps, 0 to 255 — one byte each, the same rounding the ear forgave. A pixel is therefore three numbers, and numbers can be written down, copied and sent like any others. To the machine a photograph is not a picture; it is an enormous list.

door.q: How is 255 spelled?
Sound too is numbers — measured, rounded

step.name: the grid
step.line: two million trios, one picture
step.blurb: A television frame is 1,920 columns by 1,080 rows of these trios — about two million pixels, six million numbers. There is no image in the machine anywhere, only the list; the screen is where the list is interpreted. Every photograph ever shown on a computer has been this.

door.q: Where do two million trios live?
How does a screen’s worth cross the wire?

step.name: the frame in memory
step.line: the picture lives in a block of memory
step.blurb: The six million numbers of one frame sit together in one region of memory, the frame buffer, and the screen rereads it wholesale, dozens of times a second. The picture is not in the screen; it is a block of ordinary memory, and the screen is its window.

door.q: How a circuit holds six million numbers against time.
Who owns the block of numbers?

step.name: drawing is writing
step.line: to move something, change numbers
step.blurb: Every stroke of every game and every film is arithmetic on the buffer: move a character ten pixels right and the machine adds ten across a few hundred thousand numbers, fills in behind, shades the edge. The programmers never touch a lamp. They arrange for numbers to change — and deciding which numbers change is a different, older question.

door.q: Who decides, and how? The trail of choices.
What if two programs draw at once?

step.name: the beat
step.line: whatever is in the buffer is what you see
step.blurb: A clock beats, and on each beat the screen repaints from the buffer, top to bottom, while the machine races to finish its changes before the next one. A moving image is a list rewritten in time with a clock; miss the beat and the picture tears, win it and everything moves.

door.q: The switching illusion — who repaints your world?
What holds the frame between beats?

trail.bottom: Light rounded to numbers, numbers held in memory, memory repainted in time. At the bottom, each of these numbers is spelled in the machine’s alphabet.

door.q: The Bit — the spelling of every number
The trail of the machine — what does the painting

trail.title: How a message travels
trail.intro: No wire runs from your phone to the restaurant. Your order crosses in small numbered pieces, handed from machine to machine, and is rebuilt at the far end. This is the trail of a message.

step.name: chopping
step.line: a long message becomes small packets
step.blurb: A wire can carry only so much at once, and a long message would jam every machine along its road. So the sender chops it: the order becomes a handful of small packets, a few hundred bytes each, sent separately. Nothing crosses whole; everything crosses in pieces.

door.q: Numbers all the way down — what carries them?
What are the envelopes spelled in?

step.name: the envelope
step.line: every packet labelled with numbers
step.blurb: Each piece is wrapped in an envelope — where from, where to, which piece of the whole this is — and every machine on the network has a number of its own, four bytes such as 142.250.72.14. The envelope is written in the same numbers as the message. No router can read your order; every router can read the envelope.

door.q: What is inside the machines doing the handing?
What are addresses made of?

step.name: hop to hop
step.line: no road goes all the way
step.blurb: At each crossroads a router reads the address and hands the packet down the best next wire; the route can change mid-message, and the pieces of one order may travel different roads. The internet is not a web of wires to places. It is a crowd of small machines, each deciding the next hop.

door.q: What stands at each hop?
Many packets, one wire — who goes first?

step.name: reassembly
step.line: the pieces arrive out of order and are rebuilt
step.blurb: The pieces may arrive out of order, and each envelope says which piece it is, so the receiver rebuilds the whole before anyone reads it. The number on the envelope is what makes confetti a message. Lose the numbering and no wire, however fast, can deliver an order.

door.q: Where do the pieces wait?
Who does the rebuilding?

step.name: keep until received
step.line: a copy held until the far end answers
step.blurb: A packet can vanish in a crowd, so the sender keeps a copy until the far end says received, and sends it again if the silence lasts. That one small rule lets ten thousand strangers share one planet of wires without losing their words — and it is the same rule that keeps two riders off one order.

door.q: Two hands, one order book: the oldest bug, and the cure.
A copy held — held where?

trail.bottom: Chopped, numbered, handed onward, rebuilt: everything you have ever sent travelled as numbers in envelopes.

door.q: The Bit — envelopes and addresses are numbers
The trail of the machine — what a router is

trail.title: Who runs the machine
trail.intro: Your phone seems to do twenty things at once. It does one at a time, very fast, with a manager. This is the trail of the manager.

step.name: one at a time
step.line: the processor does one thing per instant
step.blurb: However much seems to be happening, the processor executes one instruction at a time, one per beat. Two programs cannot share a moment. Every claim of simultaneity on your phone is an arrangement built on that single fact, and the arrangement has a name.

door.q: What is the one thing?
Who decides what the one thing is?

step.name: the illusion
step.line: switching so fast it looks like everything at once
step.blurb: The trick is switching: a sliver of one program, then a sliver of the next, thousands of times a second, with each one’s whereabouts kept in memory between its turns. None of them notices the gaps. The twenty simultaneous programs are a stage illusion, run very well and very fast.

door.q: The dance, billions of times a second
The switching is a decision

step.name: the scheduler
step.line: a program that decides who goes next
step.blurb: Who goes next is decided by a program, the scheduler — the one program allowed to stop the others and start them again, thousands of times a second. It is a program like any other, running on the same machine by the same rules: a shepherd that is also a sheep, merely trusted.

door.q: How does a machine decide anything at all?
Two programs, one instant — what keeps them apart?

step.name: files
step.line: named blocks of numbers on a disk
step.blurb: A program not running is a file: a named block of bytes on a disk, beside your photographs and your orders. The file is not the program, only its frozen numbers, read back into memory and continued when called. A disk is memory that does not mind waiting.

door.q: How a circuit holds anything at all.
A disk is what, exactly?

step.name: the gatekeeper
step.line: one program allowed to touch everything
step.blurb: Memory, disks, the wire, the screen: every program wants them, and only one program is allowed to hand them out — the operating system. Your apps never touch the hardware; they ask, and the manager grants or refuses. That is why one crashing app does not take the phone down with it: the failure stops at the door.

door.q: What may the one program touch?
Who stops two hands on one cell?

trail.bottom: The manager, the scheduler, the files: all of it is programs, and all programs are instructions stored and obeyed. Under the manager stands the machine itself.

door.q: The trail of the machine — what the manager runs
Time — when two hands meet one cell

trail.title: The machine itself
trail.intro: Every trail on this deck ends in a program being obeyed. This is what obeying means: the stored program, from a 1945 sketch to the phone in your hand.

step.name: the radical idea
step.line: store the instructions with the data, in advance
step.blurb: Before 1945 a machine was rewired for each new job; the program was the wiring. The idea that ended that: keep the instructions in the same memory as the data, written down in advance, and let one machine run any job by reading them. The machine no longer changes for the work. The work is a list, and the list is numbers.

door.q: The manager is stored too
How is an instruction spelled?

step.name: a number that means a command
step.line: the cell decides by position which it is
step.blurb: In memory a program looks like nothing at all: numbers in cells, indistinguishable from data. The number 108 in one cell is an instruction — load — and the same 108 elsewhere is a piece of data. The difference is not in the cell; it is where the machine is looking. Code is data, and attention makes it code.

door.q: 108 — a number like any other
Load is one of a few dozen words

step.name: the dance
step.line: fetch, decode, execute — billions of times a second
step.blurb: The machine runs one round forever: fetch the next instruction, decode what its number means — add, load, jump — execute it, move on. Billions of rounds a second, on the beat of a clock. Nothing else is happening inside the phone, the console, the router or the television; every one of them runs this one dance.

door.q: Who shares one machine among many programs?
The dance, step by step

step.name: the one design
step.line: in every box on every trail
step.blurb: The console, the courier’s phone, the warehouse server, the router, the player in the television: one design, scaled and costumed, in every box this deck has walked. Von Neumann’s group sketched it in 1945; the world has built it in the billions since, and nothing has replaced it.

door.q: The whole machine, small enough to step through
Is there anything it cannot do?

trail.bottom: One dance, in every machine you own. The whole machine, small enough to step through by hand, is a primer — and so is the question of what it can never do.

door.q: A real machine — the dance, step by step, for your hands
The Turing machine — what such a machine can never do

trail.title: How a machine decides
trail.intro: Jump if the button is pressed and the feet are on the ground. Send again if the answer never came. Grant the next slice to whoever has waited longest. Every decision a program makes is a fork, and the forks themselves are wired.

step.name: one question
step.line: every decision is yes or no
step.blurb: A program decides by asking: is the button pressed? is the count zero? is this address mine? Each question has two answers, and the program takes one road or the other. All the branching richness of software — menus, autopilots, this deck — is a braid of two-answer forks.

door.q: Yes and no — the two symbols
A question etched in sand

step.name: and, or, not
step.line: the everyday words are the wiring diagram
step.blurb: Jump if pressed AND on the ground. Fire if either button is pressed: OR. Move unless paused: NOT. The words that combine questions in daily speech are the exact ones the machine needs, and each is a small circuit of switches that answers the combined question electrically, in an instant, with nobody home.

door.q: The words, wired
Made of what?

step.name: the gate
step.line: a question etched in sand
step.blurb: That circuit is called a logic gate: a few pieces of carefully poisoned sand that turn voltages into an answer. AND, OR, NOT, and three or four cousins are the complete vocabulary of decision — the smallest parts of the machine that can be said to know anything.

door.q: The whole vocabulary, for your hands
What are gates good for?

step.name: billions of forks
step.line: the day’s work of a processor
step.blurb: Sixty times a second the game asks a few million of these questions; the scheduler asks who has waited longest; the router asks which wire is best. Every if in every program, unwound far enough, lands on gates — questions etched in sand, answered billions of times a second, honestly, because honestly is all a gate can be.

door.q: Where the forks are taken
How fast is a decision?

trail.bottom: Decision, wired. The whole vocabulary — six gates, one picture, every truth table — is a primer, and it is the piece the rest of the machine is made from.

door.q: Gates — the whole vocabulary, for your hands
The Bit — what the gates are made of

rung.name: the world in
rung.line: sensors turn the world into numbers
rung.blurb: The machine cannot know the world directly; it holds only numbers. So every entrance is a translation. A button becomes 1 or 0; a finger becomes a place on a grid; a sound becomes 44,100 measurements a second; a gust becomes a reading of pressure. Nothing enters unmeasured, and nothing enters whole. Input is the world, spelled in numbers.

door.q: How the world gets in — a song, measured

rung.name: the world out
rung.line: numbers turned back into light and sound
rung.blurb: Work done, the numbers must become the world again. A screen is a wall of lamps obeying numbers; a speaker is a cone pushed in time with them; a drone’s rotor is told a number called throttle. Output is the translation home — and it has a deadline: the world must see the finished result before the clock’s next beat, or it sees the machine thinking.

door.q: How the world gets out — a picture, repainted

rung.name: the manager
rung.line: one machine, shared among many programs
rung.blurb: Nothing you own runs one program. A manager hands out slices of the processor, keeps each program’s whereabouts between its turns, guards the memory, the disk and the wire, and refuses applications at the door. The simultaneity you see is an illusion run very fast — and the manager is the one running it.

door.q: Who runs the machine — the trail of the manager

rung.name: the program
rung.line: a promise, kept by a list of instructions
rung.blurb: To the user an application is a thing with behaviour: press this and the order goes out; tap that and the film resumes; tilt this and the helicopter holds its height. Inside it is a list, written in advance, of what to do when. Whatever a computer seems to be doing — forecasting, filming, flying — at this rung it is a list being obeyed, keeping a promise.

door.q: Two rivers — the words programs are composed from

rung.name: the code
rung.line: the list itself, written in advance
rung.blurb: Below every promise is the list. Measure, compare, correct, repeat — the loop that holds a helicopter level. Search the facts, take the best — the step that finds the nearest rider. Code is instructions stored ahead of the moment they are needed, and the machine never improvises: it walks the list, exactly, at absurd speed.

door.q: Recursion — a recipe that contains a copy of itself

rung.name: the machine
rung.line: store the program with the data, then obey it
rung.blurb: One sketch, 1945: keep the instructions in the same memory as the data, and one machine can run any job by reading them. The work is numbers; the plan is numbers; the machine no longer changes for the task. Every computer you own — phone, console, router, the drone’s little brain — is this one design, scaled and costumed.

door.q: The machine itself — the stored program

rung.name: the dance
rung.line: fetch, decode, execute — on the beat
rung.blurb: Obedience is one round dance: fetch the next instruction, decode what its number means — add, load, jump — execute it, move on. Billions of rounds a second, on the beat of a clock. The frame of the game, the packet of the stream, the correction of the helicopter all come down to this same round, danced at different speeds in different costumes.

door.q: A real machine — the dance, step by step, for your hands

rung.name: the fork
rung.line: every decision is gates etched in sand
rung.blurb: Compare, then branch: jump if the button is pressed; correct if the height is low; resend if the answer never came. Every decision is yes or no, and each yes or no is answered by a logic gate — a few grains of carefully poisoned sand turning voltages into an answer. All the branching of every program is a braid of these forks.

door.q: Every fork's yes or no is a gate — the gates themselves

rung.name: the bedrock
rung.line: two symbols, and everything spelled in them
rung.blurb: At the bottom of every rung, the same floor. The button, the pixel, the instruction, the address on the envelope: each is spelled in two symbols — 0 and 1, off and on, no and yes. Nothing sits below this. Everything above it is arrangement.

door.q: The Bit — the two symbols everything is spelled in
What is the alphabet made of — the switches that decide?

rail.name: memory
rail.blurb: One rail runs alongside every rung: numbers must be held while other numbers are computed. Held for a microsecond in a register, for a minute in a frame buffer, for a winter on a disk — the circuit that holds anything at all is one trick, scaled.

door.q: Memory — how a circuit holds anything at all

rail.name: the wire
rail.blurb: The second rail carries numbers between machines. No wire runs all the way; messages cross chopped, numbered, handed onward, rebuilt at the far end. A shared game world, a warehouse of orders, a film arriving just in time — all one trick: copies, kept in step.

door.q: How a message travels — the trail of a message

rail.name: the shared moment
rail.blurb: The third rail is the oldest bug: two hands reaching for the same thing in the same instant, with no agreed order between them. Every system that lets two actors touch one cell — an order book, a game world, a forecast written while it is read — is a scheme for making that impossible.

door.q: Time — when two hands meet one cell

pattern.intro: Whatever the thing — a game, a delivery, a film, a helicopter holding still in the wind — the answer has one shape. The world presses in; sensors turn it into numbers. Programs decide what to make of them; a manager shares the machine among them; the machine obeys stored instructions, one at a time, on the beat. The decisions bottom out in gates, the numbers in bits, and the result is turned back out into the world, in time. Every card on this deck climbs this same ladder; each only wears different weather.
pattern.bottom: Nine rungs, three rails, one bedrock. Whatever the next card on this deck is — a helicopter, a forecast, a swarm of dancing drones — it will climb this same ladder, and its parts will sit where these sit.

door.q: Gates — the whole vocabulary, for your hands
The Bit — the two symbols
